big: Before an IPO, a stranger says: 'The grey market shows a 60% listing gain. Apply now.' Rohan applies with his savings. The shares list flat. The grey market was a rumour, and a rumour is not a promise.

lines: The grey market premium looked so confident. How wrong can it be?
It is unofficial and unregulated. It can be very wrong. Treat it as noise and not as a signal. Learn the real risks instead.

rows: An unofficial price rumour, not reliable
A period when certain holders cannot sell after the IPO
A small company on a separate platform, usually riskier
A large institution that commits just before the issue opens
note: An anchor investor taking part is not a guarantee of a good price. It only shows some institutions applied.

title: Risks and cautions
stops: The grey market premium is unofficial and unreliable
A lock-in stops certain holders from selling for a time
An SME IPO is usually less risky than a large IPO
Anchor investors guarantee that the price will rise
caps: It is a rumour and not a regulated price.
Pre-IPO holders often cannot sell for a set time after listing.
Small companies on this platform are usually riskier.
Anchors show institutional interest, not a promise.

q: A message says the grey market premium means the IPO will list at a big gain. What is the right view?
opts: It is a guaranteed listing price
It is set by the exchange
It is unofficial and can be wrong
why: No listing price is guaranteed by a rumour.
SEBI does not set or endorse the grey market premium.
The exchange does not set it either, as it is unofficial.
The grey market is unregulated, so the premium is not reliable.

q: Pre-IPO investors cannot sell their shares for six months after listing. What is this called?
why: Oversubscription means more bids than shares.
A lock-in bars some holders from selling for a set time.
A split divides shares into more shares.
A codicil changes a will and has no link to an IPO at all.

q: Meena sees a small company listing on the SME platform. What is a sensible view?
opts: It is safer than large IPOs, always
It has no risk at all, ever
It is guaranteed by the exchange
why: Small companies on this platform usually carry higher risk.
It is not safer than a large IPO. It is usually riskier.
No IPO has zero risk, and SME issues have more.
An exchange does not guarantee the issue.

q: A big institution has agreed to buy shares a day before the issue opens to the public. What is it called?
why: A nominee receives an asset after a holder's death.
A surveyor assesses an insurance loss on a claim.
An anchor investor is a big institution that commits early.
An executor carries out the terms of a will.

pts: The grey market premium is a rumour. Do not rely on it.
A lock-in stops certain holders from selling for a time.
SME IPOs are usually riskier. Anchors are not a guarantee.
